Per `docs/DESIGN.md` §5 ("Why a utility process rather than the main process"), the main process is what keeps menus, tray, window creation, and native dialogs responsive, and two properties of the sync workload make it a bad host: `node:sqlite` is a synchronous API, so a catch-up batch writing several thousand rows blocks the calling thread for the duration — in main, that's a visible application stall — and FTS search over a large corpus has no useful upper bound on latency. Running the engine in a `utilityProcess` moves that blocking work off the main thread entirely, so the app shell stays responsive no matter how heavy sync or search gets.

A separate process also buys crash isolation and restartability: if the sync engine wedges or throws on a malformed frame, main can respawn it without killing the app or losing the user's windows (see the respawn handler in `apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts:123`). The renderer is excluded for the same structural reasons — a socket there dies on window reload or close, and multiple windows would mean multiple cursors and racing writers against one database — so the `utilityProcess` becomes the single owner of the WebSocket and the SQLite file, with `MessageChannelMain` letting renderers talk to it directly without proxying every read through main.
